task: This is a synthetic exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes as the fixed record: select, organize and phrase the story without inventing additional reported events, scenes, quotations or reporting activity. Write a headline and a reported feature of roughly 450–650 words in AP style for general newspaper readers about the volunteers building a long-term record of the stream through Hartham. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 18, 2026.

facts.text: The fictional Hartham Stream Watch group visits three agreed observation points along the same stream once a month.
Volunteer coordinator Jessa Vane carries a folder of earlier site photographs so volunteers can compare the same view rather than choose a new angle each visit.
The supplied field scene takes place after ordinary rainfall and describes leaves caught against a footbridge support and water covering part of a familiar stone.
Volunteers record the date, recent weather, visible conditions and the location associated with each note or sample.
The group uses agreed public observation points and landowner permissions rather than treating every stream bank as open access.
Its training tells volunteers to work from designated safe positions and not enter the stream to complete a missing observation.
Vane said, "Some months the page looks uneventful. Those pages matter when you are trying to understand what changed later."
Samples selected for laboratory work are sent through a partner college's process with labels and handling records.
A visual observation in the group's notebook is not presented as a laboratory identification of a pollutant.
The packet contains no laboratory result demonstrating contamination during the supplied visit.
A local farmer allows access to one observation point but asked the group to avoid treating the nearest land use as the presumed source of every change.
Farmer Orrin Dale said, "I would rather have a dated question we can examine than a rumor that starts with the field beside the water."
The group shares dated records with the environmental office, which decides whether a reported condition requires an official investigation.
Volunteer observations do not replace the environmental office's separate monitoring and enforcement responsibilities.
The group began after residents found that memories of earlier high water disagreed about which landmarks had been covered.
Its archive now contains both digital photographs and older paper notebooks, with gaps where visits could not safely take place.
A missed visit is marked as missing rather than filled with a guessed condition based on a nearby date.
New volunteers first accompany experienced members so site labels and observation categories are used consistently.
The partner college helps explain the difference between observations at one point and claims about the whole catchment.
The group has not published a numerical trend in pollution or claimed that its work caused a measured improvement in water quality.
A former school map marks an older footbridge that no longer serves as one of the group's current observation points.
The next public display will pair photographs from the same locations with their dates and notes, rather than select only the most dramatic water levels.

forbidden_additions: Confirmed contamination, a named polluter or a water-quality improvement result.
Permission to enter any bank or watercourse.
preserve: The patient repeat-observation work and the specific supplied field scene.
The difference between volunteer records, laboratory findings and official investigation.
Exact quotation wording and attribution when quotations are used.
